concepts.title: The Doormat Mother: Mrs Pearson's Household
concepts.definition: J.B. Priestley's play opens on Mrs Ann Pearson, a pleasant, worried housewife treated as a doormat by her family: daughter Doris snaps at her, son Cyril demands his tea, and husband George expects deference. They take her service as nature's law and give her no place in their evenings or respect.
concepts.key_idea: A mother taken for granted -- service mistaken for servility in the Pearson parlour.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp103.txt opening scenes (mrs pearson pleasant worried, doris and cyril rudeness, george pearson self importance, status of mother in family)
question_patterns: how do the pearson family members treat mrs pearson
in class 11 mother's day: why is mrs pearson called a doormat
describe doris's behaviour towards her mother
what does george pearson think of himself and how is he seen at the club
why does the family take the mother for granted
sketch the character of mrs pearson before the transformation

solution_steps.explain: Doris complains about her dress, Cyril expects served tea, and George assumes obedience -- service flows one way.
Mrs Pearson absorbs each slight with a worried smile, believing she must not offend her own family.
The comedy's problem is fixed: a mother has no status in a house she runs alone.

concepts.title: The Exchange of Personalities with Mrs Fitzgerald
concepts.definition: The bold, fortune-telling neighbour Mrs Fitzgerald proposes an exchange of personalities -- learned in the East -- and the timid mother agrees. Swapped into Mrs Pearson's body, the assertive Fitzgerald stays on to receive the family's return, ready to teach them a lesson in their own coin.
concepts.key_idea: A magical swap arms gentleness with steel -- the mother will speak in her own voice at last, borrowed or not.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp103.txt swap scenes (mrs fitzgerald fortune teller, exchange of personalities learned in the east, plan to teach the family)
question_patterns: how do mrs pearson and mrs fitzgerald exchange their personalities
in class 11 mother's day: why does mrs pearson hesitate before the swap
compare the personalities of the two women
what plan do the friends make for the family
where did mrs fitzgerald learn the trick of changing personalities
is the swap fair to the family discuss its purpose

solution_steps.explain: Fitzgerald is strong, blunt and worldly; Pearson is soft, anxious and obliging -- each envies the other's gift.
With a chant learned in the East, the personalities exchange bodies, putting steel inside the mother's frame.
The transformed Mrs Pearson waits, cards and drink in hand, for the family's return and its education.

concepts.title: The Lesson Taught and the Real Mother Restored
concepts.definition: One by one the family members meet the new Mrs Pearson: Doris is told off, Cyril is mocked for his tea-table tyranny, and George is told what the club really thinks of him. Stunned into cooperation, they finally plead with their real mother -- restored after the swap -- who agrees to keep the peace if they share the hearth with her.
concepts.key_idea: Tough love rebalances the home -- the family learns its mother's worth just as she returns to herself.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesp103.txt climax scenes (confrontations with doris cyril george, club revelation, swap reversal, family pleading with mother, changed household)
question_patterns: how does the transformed mrs pearson teach each family member a lesson
in class 11 mother's day: what does george learn about himself at the club
why do the family members plead with the real mother at the end
describe the changes in the pearson household after the events
was mrs fitzgerald's method right or wrong discuss
what is the message of the play mother's day

solution_steps.explain: Each family member meets blunt refusal where servility used to wait -- Doris scolded, Cyril needled, George deflated with the club's verdict.
Shaken, they rush to the seemingly changed mother; the personalities switch back and the real Mrs Pearson faces her humbled family.
She promises to be firm; the family promises consideration -- comedy closing on a re-balanced home.

worked_examples.question_pattern: What three revelations does the assertive Mrs Pearson deliver to the family, and what does each teach?

solution_template.explain: She refuses to be their servant and mocks their expectations, teaching that help is earned, not owed.
She reports the club's mockery of his pomposity -- puncturing vanity with fact.
Each revelation replaces taking-for-granted with respect -- the play's corrective lesson.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does Mrs Pearson, though miserable, initially resist Mrs Fitzgerald's plan? What does her hesitation reveal?

solution_template.explain: She fears offending her family and doubts the propriety of the trick.
Her resistance is the very servility that created the problem -- habit disguised as virtue.
Priestley shows that the oppressed must first consent to be strong; the swap only lends her borrowed courage.
